property_summary: For any caller, the reference contract's owner() always returns the fixed stored owner address (the deployer set in constructor), whereas the mutant returns the caller address making owner() caller-dependent; thus owner() == deployer for all callers in reference but not in mutant for some caller.
For any caller, C.owner() returns the current stored owner address (not always zero); the mutant that forces owner() to always return address(0) violates this when the stored owner is non-zero.

For any caller address, C.owner() returns the stored owner address (the owner set at construction or via transferOwnership); the mutant that always returns address(this) violates this because owner() will sometimes differ from the stored owner.

Invariant: transferOwnership may never set owner to the zero address — in the reference contract calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always reverts (fails) if newOwner == address(0) (so owner never becomes zero), whereas the mutant removes that check and allows setting owner to zero for some input address(0).

For any address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference contract either succeeds and sets owner to newOwner when newOwner != address(0), or reverts (so owner remains non-zero); the mutant allows setting owner to address(0) (zero address) — so there exists an input newOwner == address(0) where the mutant's owner becomes zero but the reference never allows that.

For any caller x and any proposed newOwner address a, either transferOwnership(a) reverts (so owner remains non-zero) or it succeeds and owner() == a; the buggy mutant allows a successful call that sets owner() == address(0) for some input a (zero address) while the reference always prevents setting owner to zero.

For any caller addr, only the current owner can successfully transfer ownership; the reference reverts when a non-owner calls transferOwnership, whereas the mutant also allows a non-owner call to succeed (because setting owner to zero can be exploited by calling from a zero-owner scenario), so there exist fuzzed caller addresses that distinguish them.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference contract either reverts if newOwner==address(0) or succeeds and sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant allows a successful call that sets owner() to address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner==address(0), so there exists an input (newOwner==address(0)) where owner()==address(0) after the call in the mutant but never in the reference.

For any caller who is the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) should succeed for any non-zero newOwner (i.e. allow transferring ownership to any address including non-zero); the mutant wrongly forbids non-zero newOwner causing transferOwnership to revert whenever newOwner != address(0).

For any caller address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract only succeeds (does not revert) when msg.sender == owner; the mutant inverts this check so a non-owner can successfully call transferOwnership, which the property detects by fuzzing caller and newOwner.

Invariant: only the contract owner (set at construction) can successfully call transferOwnership; the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner caller to change owner, violating this rule for some caller addresses.
After calling setRewardDistributor(x), rewardDistributor equals the provided argument (not zero) and UpdatedRewardDistributor emitted with that argument.
